a2-past-katab.title: Past Tense: I Wrote, You Saw...
a2-past-katab.explanation: Levantine past tense uses suffixes on the verb stem: كتبت (katabt, "I wrote"), كتبت (katabt, "you-m wrote"), كتبتِ (katabti, "you-f wrote"), كتب (katab, "he wrote"), كتبت (katbit, "she wrote"), كتبنا (katabna, "we wrote"), كتبتو (katabtoo, "you-all wrote"), كتبو (katabo, "they wrote"). "I" and "you-m" share the exact same form — context tells them apart.
a2-past-katab.fact: The verb شاف (shaf, "to see") follows the same suffix pattern, but as a "hollow" root (ش-و-ف) its long vowel shortens in every person except he/she/they: شفت (shift, "I saw"), شاف (shaf, "he saw"), شافت (shafit, "she saw"), شافو (shafo, "they saw") — the same aa→i shortening pattern found across hollow verbs in Arabic dialects generally.

a2-past-negation.title: Negating the Past: Ma + Past Verb
a2-past-negation.explanation: To negate a past-tense verb, put ما (ma) right before it: ما شفت (ma shift, "I didn't see"). This is the same ما used for present-tense negation — unlike مش, which is reserved for nominal/participle sentences ("أنا مش تعبان").
a2-past-negation.fact: In fast speech, ما often contracts right onto the verb with barely a pause — ماشفت — but it's still written and thought of as two separate words, ما and شفت, not a single fused word.

dialogue.en: No, I didn't see a friend today, I only saw a house

a2-days-past.title: Days of the Week with Past Tense
a2-days-past.explanation: Combining a day name with a past-tense verb builds a simple narrative: يوم الجمعة شفت صديق (yom el-jum3a shift sadeeq, "On Friday I saw a friend"). The day name simply comes first, like a time adverb.
a2-days-past.fact: Just like مبارح (yesterday), day names need no extra preposition ("on Friday") — Syrian Arabic places time expressions directly at the start of the sentence.
